summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap for a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar to change a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read in public and at the border under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment has been in force since 2007. What that protection reaches in practice is not set out in the sources: whether it covers service refusal, harassment, goods and facilities, or only employment is unresolved here.

Criminal-law protection runs on a separate footing and has moved further. Parliament amended the Crimes Act 2011 in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime, with assent on 25 September and commencement on 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending the hate crime and hate speech legislation to add protections for transgender identity, giving gender identity its own footing in the criminal law for the first time. A companion bill passed the same month makes it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy.

Family and partnership recognition is established rather than contested. Civil partnerships have existed since 2014 and same-sex marriage since December 2016, when the bill passed unanimously following a December 2015 consultation that had left the population divided. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 breached the Gibraltar Constitution, after a long-term lesbian couple refused an adoption challenged the restriction; the law was amended through the 2014 civil-partnership legislation, and the Adoption Act 2023, in full effect from 18 April 2024, expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt. Altruistic non-commercial surrogacy has been permitted for married couples and civil partners since February 2021, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived by artificial insemination, and the Gibraltar Health Authority extended assisted reproduction to lesbian couples in June 2017. A trans visitor travelling with a partner or children should not expect family status to be the source of difficulty; identity documents are.

The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender, set by the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011 after the Supreme Court held on 8 April 2011 that the former age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional; the equalised age took effect on 23 November 2012.

Oversight comes from outside as well as within. The United Kingdom House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2007-08 report on Overseas Territories set accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar, and its 2008 inquiry recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal across all overseas territories.
tangentialFactors:
Hostility to LGBT people is documented in Gibraltar even where the statute is protective. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation tackling what it called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' after an incident of anti-gay abuse; the Chief Minister used the same phrase of social-media abuse during Pride month, and the Justice Ministry opened an investigation into a proposal to make denigration on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence. No outcome for that proposal is recorded in the sources.

The trajectory of the law is toward expansion rather than restriction. Sexual activity was decriminalised in 1993, the equal age of consent arrived in 2012, adoption rights followed the 2013 constitutional ruling, civil partnerships in 2014 and marriage in 2016, and gender identity entered the hate-crime framework only in July 2026. A visitor assessing current risk should weigh the recentness of that last step: trans identity has been a protected characteristic in Gibraltar's criminal law for months, not years.

Comparatively, Gibraltar's own Parliament has moved further on recognition and family law than the United Kingdom's framework would require of it, while the United Kingdom's newer service-sector guidance has no application here absent an extension. The gap between the two regimes is therefore not uniform in one direction.
localsOnly:
Residents hold a settled set of family entitlements: civil partnership since 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016, adoption without discrimination under the Adoption Act 2023 in full effect from 18 April 2024, altruistic non-commercial surrogacy for married couples and civil partners since February 2021 with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination, and access to assisted reproduction for lesbian couples under the Gibraltar Health Authority's June 2017 policy change.

Residents also have criminal-law recourse that a visitor may not think to invoke: hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation have been a hate crime since October 2013, transgender identity was added to the hate crime and hate speech legislation in July 2026, and offering or practising conversion therapy became an offence under a bill passed the same month. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender reassignment has been unlawful since 2007.

Residents have no domestic route to change a legal gender marker, which affects local documentation, and the scope of the 2007 discrimination protection in areas such as services, goods and facilities, and harassment is not defined in the sourced material.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the practical scope of the 2007 discrimination protection. The sources do not state whether it reaches service refusal, harassment, and goods and facilities, or is confined to employment.

Unresolved: whether the July 2026 hate-crime amendment and the conversion-therapy bill received assent and are in force, and what conduct the conversion-therapy offence covers. The sources record passage by Parliament only.

Unresolved: whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or its 2025 single-sex-services code has been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council. No extension appears in the sourced material, and none is asserted here.

Not sourced: any enforcement record for the hate-crime provisions, any data on reporting rates, and whether residents of Gibraltar may seek gender recognition under United Kingdom legislation. No claim is made either way on those points.
